utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I'd like to deal with a few procedural matters before we start with the examination of the witness. First, for Witness Grekulovic no public summary is yet available and therefore should be filed, or has it been filed meanwhile?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I thought it had been filed but we'll take of that straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could be that this is -- my list is not updated. I hadn't checked it just prior to the session. Could the Stanisic Defence already inform the Chamber whether Witnesses DST-071 and 081 are to be dropped or whether you maintain them on your list.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We maintain them on the list but with this indication that DST-081 is most unlikely to come. We, to be frank, have not been able to contact him for some time, so we are not expected him to come but I would just like to keep the option open in case he makes a reappearance which he has an inclination to do. DST-071 we are checking what precise date he is available. We expect him to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I then already invite the other parties to either start thinking about the giving of evidence out of turn. I think the Prosecution was not very much in favour of allowing witnesses to give their evidence out of turn. We do not know, of course, when witness DST-071 is expected to appear, but is there anything you would like to say about it, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, obviously our preference would be that the Stanisic case finishes, but we have, I think, demonstrated our flexibility if there is compelling reasons that that should not be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the Simatovic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of the accused Simatovic is in the same position as the Prosecution. We would like the Stanisic case to be completed, but if that is impossible, then we are prepared to bring our first witness next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just to remind Your Honours, when we spoke to the -- this particular witness, last he said January was the earliest he could come, so we are anticipating that he will commit to January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll further follow this up. Then I think the OTP would like to have its submissions and requests on the dead-lines for the Stanisic Defence bar table motions, to have them on the record. I refer to an e-mail sent, I think it was on the 29th of November -- sent by Thomas Laugel to many others, in which, and I try to summarise, Mr. Groome -- in which the Prosecution insists on the Stanisic Defence following the procedure for bar table motions as the procedure as set out in the Chamber's guidance, guidance given on the 19th of February, 2010, and the 5th of July, 2010, for the filing of the bar table motions. It mainly being that the appropriate practice is that bar table motions should be made as joint submissions including the comments of both parties as to the relevance and authenticity of the charge, and in relation to that, after having set out that the Prosecution has followed this guidance, the Prosecution requests that one week per 100 documents should be given to prepare the comments. And apart from that, your request that the present portions of the unredacted requests for existence and the responses, that these pertinent portions would be provided to the Office of the Prosecution. And the last part of the request is that the request itself be put on the record, and even an offer to do it if the Chamber would so request. I think I summarised the basics of the requests; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, with one exception. It's only the pertinent portions of the RFA that we are requesting. It's not the RFAs in total but simply the portions that are necessary for us to valuate the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the pertinent portions of the unredacted RFA requests and responses. That's ... Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is what we are doing, but we would ask that we be able to do it in the timetable indicated by Your Honour, which is, I think the 15th for the first two and then the 9th of January for the third. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have the first draft, so the first tables already being presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Not the tables but the list of the documents for the first and the second have been supplied to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's how many documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Off the top of my head I'm not sure, but it's probably -- it's probably about 600, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And when they were provided?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The first was -- the first was provided last week and I think the second was provided yesterday ... [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means for 600 documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that's approximately six weeks, one week per 100 documents, and then looking at the time-limits, I don't know which parts should appear in the December portion. If that's more than 200, then it might not be easy to -- for the Prosecution to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It is more than 200. That's the larger document, I think. The larger list. Le me just try to get the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The list is not helpful because the list is only a list of 65 ter numbers. It doesn't include any information about origin or authenticity or relevance. So for us to respond to that is not possible. So what we are -- what we were talking about is not -- and, by the way, the list also has changed so they submitted it and then they made several revisions, which I understand they are working on it, so that's not the problem, but the problem is that the 100 documents per week would be from the moment that we receive the table, that includes the information about origin, authenticity and relevance, then we can begin our own review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, the lists not providing the necessary relevant information, it's one; and the second is the numbers and the time the Prosecution would have available to prepare its comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's right, the list doesn't contain that information. That's the time-consuming part. I understood from the discussion in the court last week that by providing a list that would give the Prosecution a head start they would be able to look at the documents, many of which are from their own 65 ter list, in fact, I would say a good 50 per cent are -- and if not more, and be able to say whether they accept origin and relevance, which is, on the face of many of the documents, quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, if they were on your own 65 ter list, then perhaps it's less troublesome.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, for those documents that are from our 65 ter list, I would agree. We would like to know what the relevance is so that we can express our position, but I agree with that for our 65 ter list. For those that are their 65 ter documents, however, we would definitely need the additional information before we review, otherwise we are doing a review of the documents twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I do understand, Mr. Jordash, that, as you said, that's -- what we are doing at this moment is correct and at the same time it's done at such a pace and with such timing that joint filings to be received by the Chamber - when was it - the first, on the 15th of December, I think, is almost impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I hadn't understood that that was the dead-line, that we had to do a joint filing on that date, but that might be my misunderstand but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But bar table motions are to be filed and the format as found in the guidance by the Chamber, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, yes, I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, what for us to do, to have a bar table motion which is incomplete and no one, the Chamber, of course, is -- want -- wants to know what is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. It was only my understanding that we had to -- like I say, I might have misunderstood this but it was my understanding that we had to provide the relevant charts to the Prosecution on those dates. We are -- everybody on the team other than myself and an intern is working on it. And they are working seven days a week to get it done. I mean, it really is an impossible task to do it any faster. But everybody is planning to finish off the year in a rather unpleasant way to get this finished. The volume is massive and we are doing what we can. There's simply no more resources to call upon to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll further consider it. Mr. Jordash, you have raised a few matters last week about the health of Mr. Stanisic. The Chamber staff has followed up with you and one of the consequences of this follow-up was that you suggested eight questions to be put to the reporting medical officer. The Prosecution has not objected to these questions and the Chamber will ask OLAD to instruct the reporting medical officer to address these questions in his next weekly report, and there is a possibility that we would add one or two questions to those.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I can inform Your Honours that Mr. Stanisic's new treatment commenced yesterday. He was taken to the Bronovo hospital and provided with the new medication, and, so, to that degree there's been some resolution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And one question, therefore, is: Does it need an answer anymore, is it? When does the -- I think that was one of the questions [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, that has been dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... new medication. One of the -- one of the additional questions for me would be: I've got no idea what exactly the reasons are that this medication has to be started in hospital rather than in another situation, whether there's -- whether this has any effect on Mr. Stanisic's health. Again, I'm not interesting -- interested in the details, but if the start of the medication -- how to administer the medication, if that's to be done in hospital, of course, the immediate question is whether this has any effect on -- if only temporarily, on his well-being.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. I can perhaps cast a little light in that Your Honours may recall last year the beginning of similar treatment and a reaction in the UNDU, and I -- I'm supposing but I don't know that because the treatment is similar, although different, that caution has been exercised this time and he receives [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Rather to -- so then the main reason would be not the way in which the medication is administered, but rather to monitor very carefully and from very closely the possible effect of the new medication when administered for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just take a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's the case, to monitor the two new medication that he has taken and I think the reaction he had last year was at the beginning and so the recommendation is now to have the monitoring at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And since it started yesterday, any specific matter to report, or at this moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, my co-counsel saw Mr. Stanisic today and he seemed to be in much finer form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's good to hear anyhow. That's ... Then I move on to the next item. Serbia has requested transcripts of the 21st of November. The request was to be provided for the transcripts of the 54 bis hearing of the 21st of November, and first of all, most of this hearing was held in public session and is, therefore, available on the Tribunal's website, but there are also two private session parts, and the Registry is hereby instructed to provide Serbia with these parts, these parts being transcript pages 15022, line 24, until 15031, line 22. That was the first portion. And the second being 15052, line 19, up to 15057, line 24. And the Registry is also instructed to inform the Republic of Serbia of the Chamber's decision I just rendered. I put on the record some developments in relation to the Brown expert report. The Stanisic Defence had requested that the dead-line for Friday, Mr. Brown's report, was moved to the 15th of December, 2011. The Prosecution had also requested to be provided with the draft report but as no such draft report is in the Stanisic Defence's possession, the Chamber denied that request. Perhaps unnecessary to add to this, Mr. Jordash, that the Trial Chamber was not really amused to receive a request for an extension of time on the very day the dead-line expired.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, and we apologise for that. We did our best to contact the expert but couldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's quite amazing these days that you can't get hold of someone for such a relatively long period of time in this modern times where communication seems to be possible every minute of the day, every day of the week. I'm not blaming you for it, but if you can't make a dead-line, then perhaps you should make yourself a bit better available for those who may want to inquire into that, meeting the dead-line. Then the next and the last one on my list, the Stanisic Defence has urgently requested provisional release for Mr. Stanisic. Are you considering to request leave to reply, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not sure whether the Chamber inadvertently omitted to give its ruling with respect to the Brown report, but having spoken about it, I don't see on the record any decision with respect to that extension request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we moved to the 15th but we'll check where exactly is to be found, Mr. Groome, and if we only agreed without informing the parties in an appropriate way then we'll correct that as and as possible. I have no further procedural matters on my list. Is the ... is the Stanisic Defence ready to continue its cross-examination of witness Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could he be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Milovanovic. I would like to invite you to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovanovic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, you are not here for the first time in this case. It was developments that happened after you testified which caused the parties to call you back to further examine you on matters which were not already available at the time of your examination in April 2001 [sic]. You'll first now be further cross-examined by Mr. Jordash, and as you know by now, Mr. Jordash is counsel for Mr. Stanisic. Mr. Jordash, are you ready? Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so there's no confusion and this witness has testified in other cases, I believe you misspoke when you said "2001," you meant "2010" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I intended to say 2010, as a matter of fact, that I said April, I think I added, and it was April 2010, so that's what I had on my mind. And I talked about in this case. Mr. Jordash, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You were given a number of files, I hope, yesterday. Did you have an opportunity to read through them. I know there was quite a lot to get through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I perhaps -- Mr. Milovanovic, the Chamber is aware that you asked for a postponement of your testimony so that you could read it all. We have decided that we would start with your examination even if you would not have read it all, so, therefore, don't feel guilty in any way of not having digested, which, as far as was reported to the Chamber, which seems to be quite a lot of material. But perhaps you answer the question of Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be heard, please. Already in Banja Luka I learned that there would be some materials waiting for me here. They asked me if I wanted the materials to be on a CD or on paper, and I requested a hard copy. Yesterday when I arrived there were three binders waiting for me, 400 pages long. I managed to go through one until 11.00 in the evening. I went halfway through the second one and I did not even manage to open the third one. I'm telling you this just so that you know what I've been able to read. The first one I read through; the second one-half way; the third one I didn't even touch because, well, it was physically impossible to go through all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And thank you very much for the effort. I'm sorry to have put you under such time constraints. Let's see where we can get to. First of all, before I return to the Mladic diaries, let me just indicate what I would like to do, which is, in the main, take you through some of the Mladic diaries and see if you have any knowledge of certain things described in there, and see if you are able to elaborate on some of the things that are in there. That's going to be the principal focus. Before we turn to the diaries, could I just ask you, though, to look at a map which has been prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please, could we have on the screen 1D05282.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what is going to come on the screen is a map with four locations marked. And for your information, these are the locations of airfields which were referred to in the combat readiness and activities of the Army of the VRS in 1992 dated April of 1993. Now, as you look at that map, am I correct that you had a -- played a role in drafting the combat readiness and activities analysis of the VRS in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Which is, Your Honours, P386.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I'm looking at the map, I can see four airports: Mahovljani, which is an airport where combat aircrafts and helicopters were based; next to it, in the direction of Banja Luka some 20 kilometres away, is Zaluzani airport. This airport was built before the war. It was a military airport and during the war this was a helicopter base; Prijedor airport is exclusively a sports airport. It still exists, and it is intended for smaller aircraft, for example, a Cessna. It was not a combat airport; and then Bratunac airport is also a sports airport. It belongs to an -- a club. During the war it was an auxiliary airport and it could be used for combat activities but for very special aircraft; there is another auxiliary airport missing from the map. Before the war, the name of that airport near Glamoc was Ivo Lola Ribar and during the war we referred to it as only Glamoc airport and this was intended for forcible take-offs and landings of aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I ask you please to indicate with a pen on the map where that other airport was, please, the one that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking for Glamoc. I can't see Glamoc in this part of the map. I think that the map should be moved on the screen to the right, perhaps Glamoc will be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps we can save some time, Mr. Milovanovic, and come back to this. Perhaps during a break we can give you map and you can mark that.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, in the left bottom corner, there is a village called Crni Lug. I can no longer see it, actually. Here it is, Crni Lug. Ticevo and Glamoc should be somewhere around this area known as Nakovanj in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in a valley where I'm pointing with a pen. Currently, Glamoc is in the territory of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is no longer in the territory of Republika Srpska. And the second part of your question was whether I participated in the drafting of the analysis of combat readiness for --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Before we move to that, could you just indicate with a round circle the location of the airport that you've referred to, then we can move from that first question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the right pen -- yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I can see three lines of pen on the map now. Which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the last one the witness marked is at the very left of the map. He first referred to Crni Lug where there is a small marking, but the biggest marking just on the -- the one closest to Prijedor, south of Prijedor, is the one he marked as the location of the airport, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. And the second question was: Did you participated in the drafting of the combat report?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the Chief of the Main Staff during the war and all combat reports and all the analysis of combat readiness had to go through the staff, which means that I participated in the drafting of all those.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. These five airfields, were these the five airfields that were used by the VRS during the conflict in Bosnia? Were there any others that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prijedor airfield was not used in combat or for combat, I already stated that. Bratunac airport was used in the course of 1992, during the first few months of the war, and only for propellor aircraft, and an airfield near Glamoc was an auxiliary airport which was not used for combat. However, if the air force was active in Herzegovina and could not reach Banja Luka this is where they would land to refuel. For example, aircraft of a Jastreb type with could not fly as far, whereas the aircraft of Orao type could fly even further. In any case, Mahovljani airport was used for landing and take-off of air force. And let me just tell you that the air force of Republika Srpska was used during the first part of -- first few months of the war after the decision was reached by the international community in London sometime in October 1992. And then the air force was landed forever, we discussed the possibility of dismantling our air force or perhaps move it to Yugoslavia, and we decided that it would remain in Mahovljani but that it would be permanently grounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. You've asked a question or some questions that I was going to ask you. Just so that we are clear, were there any other airfields which were in any way used by the VRS in relation to either combat supplies, or humanitarian supplies before the air force was grounded?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A sports airport existed in the vicinity of Bijeljina. I don't remember that it was ever used for combat, just like the one near Prijedor. I don't remember any other airfields. The commander actually transferred all the issues with -- regarding the use of air force to me as his deputy. We started building an airfield in Podromanija, at the crossroads of roads between Rogatica, Sokolac and Pale. But the land was just marked and that was the end of all the works, and that's how the situation is even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And so that never started operating; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was never built. It was never used, therefore. It was only designed. I suppose that was an attempt on the part of the government of Republika Srpska to compete with the Federation because the Federation has two airports, one in Sarajevo the other in Tuzla, so I suppose that the government of Republika Srpska wanted to build their own, but it is by no means an easy task to build a fully operational airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And each of the airfields that you referred to as being used by the VRS were under the - let me put it differently -- were owned and secured and used by the VRS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all unnecessary microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only Mahovljani and Zaluzani airports and the auxiliary airport near Glamoc. They were under the military administration. Zaluzani airport before the war belonged to the JNA, but it was slowly abandoned after Mahovljani airport was constructed because Mahovljani airport was a combined airport for military and civil aircrafts. Since civil aircrafts disappeared at the beginning of war in the territory of modern Republika Srpska, Mahovljani remained exclusively a military airfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. When the no-fly zone was imposed by the United Nations, your, as you've said, air fleet was grounded. Am I correct that the only flights thereafter in VRS territory were helicopters being used to air-lift wounded from the front lines to hospitals?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When no-fly zone was imposed, medical helicopters were excluded from the decision. They had to be clearly marked with a red cross. And also we were allowed to transport materials but all such flights had to be previously announced with UNPROFOR. I know that immediately after the decision was made in London, UNPROFOR placed its monitors in Mahovljani airport to observe the no-fly zone agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. When was the no-fly zone imposed and when did it become effective in the way you've just described?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Discussions about imposing the no-fly zone on Republika Srpska started in October 1992. And I believe that on the 31st of March, 1993, a resolution of the Security Council was passed and according to that resolution, the decision was implemented. I don't remember the number of the resolution, but I know that it became effective on the 31st of March, 1993. And that decision also prescribed all the other possible uses of aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move to another subject. I just want to touch on your interaction with Mladic so we can understand perhaps a little more about these notebooks. When you were first promoted, you - is this right? - went to the Assembly of the RS on the 12th of May with Mladic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What rank do you have in mind when you have that I was promoted into a rank? What rank would that be?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you about what happened on the 12th of May when you went to Banja Luka and you were promoted; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could we have a year, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 1992, sorry. Major-general.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became major-general on the 26th April 1992. At that time I was in Nis. And then pursuant to an order, I was transferred to the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo on the 8th of May, 1992. However, I never arrived in Sarajevo. I arrived in Han Pijesak on the 11th of May, 1992. And that same afternoon I met with Mladic and the other members of the future Main Staff. On the 12th there was a session of the Assembly in Banja Luka which I did not attend, and thank you for the materials that you left with me yesterday, it was only last night that I managed to read Mladic's speech at that session of the Assembly. General Mladic, Colonel Tolimir, Colonel Gvero and General Djukic went to that session which means that almost all Mladic's assistants but me went there, and I stayed behind to organise the work of the Main Staff. On the eve of that day we assembled for the first time, so I was told to organise communications with our subordinated units that we had at the time and to start receiving reports from the field. Effectively, on the 12th of May, the war actually started for the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I got the impression that you wanted to know whether the witness went with Mr. Mladic on the 12th of May to the Assembly. I've approximately two and a half minutes of information which seems to be a long no-answer, we know what he did all this time. Could you please try to keep the witness to what you really want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you said you didn't attend the 12th of May Assembly session, Mr. Milovanovic. Did you go together with Mr. Mladic on that day to Banja Luka where that -- was it in Banja Luka that the Assembly was held? Yes. Did you go with Mr. Mladic to Banja Luka on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then in your previous answer, if you just have answered I didn't go to the Assembly session, I didn't go to Banja Luka on the 12 of May, that would have been one line where we now read 20 lines; perhaps useful information, I do not know, perhaps Mr. Jordash knows, but certainly not an answer to the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You mentioned there in your answer that you were left behind and were left behind, in part, to take charge of establishing communication with subordinate units. Was that a task which was yours from that time onwards in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief of any staff is always responsible for the functioning of communication in any military.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you understand that in that role you were to pursue certain VRS goals, one of those goals being to protect the Serb people and territory, and the other was to deal with paramilitaries, to name just two for the moment?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And which subordinates would report directly to you in that role?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the establishment of communication, the person responsible and who reported to me was Colonel Radomir Role a member of the Main Staff. As for the paramilitaries, the entire Main Staff was responsible, including the commander. I was the one who drafted orders and submitted them to subordinated officers, and in the field it was the commanders in every particular area that were responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you told by Mladic at this point in time that the VRS consisted of about 80- to 90.000 personnel with arms?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In terms of how often from that time onwards you saw Mladic, did you have meetings with him on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Crna Rijeka where the Main Staff was based, Mladic and I shared an office due to the scarcity of space. We practically shared one desk, we had two chairs, which means that we saw each other every day when he was in the office because we worked in the same office.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you would have morning meetings which would be attended by Mladic and certain commanders and their assistants; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every morning between 6.00 and 7.00 the Main Staff received reports from subordinates. It would be either General Mladic or myself who received them. And then from 7.00 onwards we had our regular Main Staff briefings. And we also had meetings of the inner Main Staff which means Mladic and the seven of us assistants. We analysed the developments that took place the previous days and we made plans for the following day, which means that we met twice a day. If Mladic was there, he would head those meetings. If he was absent, it would be myself, and vice-versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you would receive daily combat reports from subordinated units from within VRS territory on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we received those reports before 2000 hours. However, since the reports provided an overview of the situation as of 1700 hours, the commander of the brigade would submit reports to the corps commander. The corps commander would read reports from all the brigades, and then he would compile his own report for the Main Staff, and then the subordinated commanders reported by telephone after 2200 hours to provide updates on the written reports. Based on those reports, the Main Staff had to submit a written combat reports of the Army of the Republika Srpska to the Supreme Command or the supreme commander, President Karadzic, before 2400 hours each day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And just so we are clear, you would receive reports about the full range of VRS activities and activities within VRS territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Including logistics, personnel issues, training issues, combat operations? You received reports on all of those things on a daily or regular basis; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There is a regulation based on which reports are compiled. The first set of information is on the enemy. The second part is on what the subordinated corps did, what the plans are for the following day, the following part is about issues and problems. I believe that there were seven different items to cover and the last item would be requests upon the superior command regarding fuel, ammunition, and similar things, as well as report on casualties, i.e., the number of wounded, the number of missing, the number of dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. And in terms of Mladic and his note-taking, how regular did it seem, to you at the time, that he was taking notes?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I spoke about that even the last time. Every officer, when he graduates from the military academy and comes to a unit, receives a so-called work notebook where he writes every day the tasks that he had been given so as not to forget anything more important that happened in his unit especially if he commands the unit, as every clerk would do, and it's not just a habit but an obligation of every officer to keep notes. Mladic and I did the same, although we shared a desk, and every soldier in the Army of Republika Srpska did the same. Those are not war diaries. It's something different. Those are notes that helped remind you of a task you received or a proper way to solve a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So that's what we are talking about in relation to the Mladic diaries that you've seen -- that you saw on this here before coming to court today, and also that you looked at when you attended this trial before? We are talking about his -- sorry, Mr. Groome is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know whether Mr. Groome wants to wait until you have finished your question or whether -- Mr. Groome, is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, now that -- I am sorry to have interrupted, but I think there's a risk of confusion. I think the witness's last answer shows this. There are two documents: One is called "notebooks" and one is called "diaries." The books that have been given to the witness, I believe, I have not seen what was given last night, but are notebooks and not diaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That is what I was about to ask the witness just to clarify that. Yes, and the witness is nodding.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So the Mladic material that you've looked at, that we are all talking about, are his personal notebooks from what you can see from looking at them?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did you notice then with him a continuous habit of writing in this notebook?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have to notice it during the war but I did see those notebooks when they were given to -- for me to see in court, and I had to see that he apparently did it every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, that's not my question. My question is: Did you notice him doing it? Would you have noticed if he had stopped doing it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's take it step by step, is it, Mr. Jordash. Did you see Mr. Mladic on a regular basis writing in his notebook?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. I saw him either writing in it or reading from it. If he had prepared for a meeting in advance then he always did that in that work notebook and from it he would read to us the tasks that he was going to give us. And if he wasn't reading, he was writing in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you say if he wasn't reading he was writing, did you mean that you saw him writing on a daily basis in those notebooks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And as long as you were close to him, you would, therefore, have observed if he would not have done that anymore, of course, if he was away you couldn't observe anything, but did he do this as -- during all the time you were close to him able to observe what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Throughout the war, I sat to the left of Mladic, shoulder to shoulder, and I was always able to see whether he was writing or not. And when we were apart he was usually at a meeting, either at the Supreme Command or somewhere else, or meeting with a subordinate unit. And he kept notes everywhere, and on his return, he would always inform the Main Staff, or if not the Main Staff, then me, reading from his notebook all the notes that he had taken at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, I appreciate from what you've told us before that you were not with him during the events in Srebrenica in 1995, during the massacres there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beginning with the 28th of October 1994 until 15 October 1994, I was not with Mladic all the time. I was in the west in Drvar and Banja Luka, whereas Mladic remained in Han Pijesak and all that happened around Srebrenica. I was not with him around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can you think of any reason, though, why from your communication with him around that time he might not have made any notes about those events?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why he didn't. I don't remember. He didn't even talk to me about Srebrenica. When I returned, it was some sort of secret around the Main Staff. He didn't discuss it, and whether he had kept notes there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, before we turn to the diary, I just want to ask you how you went about in May of 1992 and thereafter subordinating the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I spoke about that in my last testimony, but I'll repeat it briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. -- I don't want you to repeat what you've said, I just want to know -- let me ask more specific questions. Was there a clear plan laid out to subordinate paramilitaries within VRS territory?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No plan was made. It was a decision of the Main Staff that read, roughly speaking, I can't quote it verbatim but approximately, call in for a discussion all the commanders of the military forces of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- sorry, of the paramilitary forces, and offer them the following: to become part of the VRS in their respective territories. If they do not want to integrate with the VRS because most of these paramilitaries were from outside the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then return to where they came from. If they want to integrate with the VRS, their fighting men can individually join units of the VRS. Those who refuse both, that means to leave the BH territory or to join the VRS on an individual basis, will be expelled. Those who offer armed resistance, will be destroyed. That meeting occurred just after the session in Banja Luka and General Mladic and Tolimir, as chief of the security and intelligence, attended as well as General Gvero, who was in charge of moral guidance and religious affairs. Major Ljubisa Savic, known as Mauzer, who was commander of the Panthers, a volunteer brigade, integrated the VRS first under the command of the Main Staff, then the Eastern Bosnia Corps. Arkan with his Tigers refused, and he went back to Serbia, and from there I don't know where else. Many border municipalities had their own TO units established by the ruling party, the SDS. All of those units, I believe there were 92 of them, 92 brigades, integrated with the VRS. There was one group around Zvornik commanded by a certain Zuca and Crni and Captain Dragan, that I spoke about last time, that did not join the VRS. We expelled and arrested those men, broke them up, in any case. On the 28th of June, an order by the Main Staff was written and signed by General Mladic, I believe I wrote it personally, and in that order all that we had previously agreed and tried to carry out ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You said 28th of June, did you mean the 28th of July?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: June.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, my mistake. When do you say, from what you recall, that all -- let me rephrase that. 28th of July -- sorry, 28th of June, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What date would you suggest was the date when all paramilitaries that remained within Bosnia were fully and finally integrated into the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which day of the week it was, I don't know, but I know the 28th of June is a Serbian religious holiday, Vidovdan, and it's the patron saints day for the VRS. We had to get legal grounds for breaking up that group around Zvornik and several groups around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, I've got a lot of material to get through, so if you could answer more directly, that would be great. What date do you say was the date when all existing paramilitaries had left or were integrated into the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paramilitary units started disappearing from the 12th of May until 28th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm asking quite a specific question. What date do you say, if you know, was the date when all existing paramilitaries had left or were integrated into the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you the date. Mauzer joined the VRS as soon as he made a contact with General Mladic. Now, I don't know when General Mladic, Tolimir or Gvero spoke to the next commander of the paramilitary unit, that is to say Arkan. At the time when they spoke to Arkan and he refused to join the VRS, he was ordered to leave the territory of Republika Srpska and he did. I cannot now remember any other paramilitary unit. After Zuca and Crni around Zvornik were spoken to, they didn't want to leave Republika Srpska either because they were natives of that territory, nor did they want to join --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, you are describing the whole history. The only thing Mr. Jordash asked you is: Can you give me a date on which those who did not want to be integrated had left and the others had been subordinated, integrated into the VRS. Can you give a date for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't tell you the date because I don't know when Mladic spoke to each of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The simple answer is no, I can't give you a date. It's as simple as that, Mr. Milovanovic. Why you can't give a date is another matter, if Mr. Jordash wants to know, he will ask you, but the simple answer is: No, I can't give a date for that. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. And just so that we are clear, when you say integrated into the VRS, integrated means they are subordinated to and receive their supplies from the VRS, does that sum up what you mean by integrated?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they joined and integrated into the VRS in all aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I notice the time, Your Honour. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take a break and resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, one short observation. The dead-line, having moved to the 15th of December, was communicated to the parties in an e-mail sent, I think, on the 2nd of December. It was not put on the record yet. That's where we stand, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I thought that you meant to when you were discussing it at that time, that's why I didn't see it, that's why I brought to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is hereby on the record, and the parties were informed on the 2nd of December in an informal communication by e-mail. Mr. Jordash, we have now -- for a long time we have a marked map somewhere which is not tendered, I don't know what you want to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I tender it, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be D559, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Milovanovic, could you try to focus your answer on what is specifically asked. If we need further explanation, then we will ask you for further explanation or further details. So if someone asks you whether you arrive here by a red car, then don't tell us that approximately 10 per cent of the cars are red in the Netherlands and that, apart from being red, it had four tires and that it drove at a speed of, et cetera. Just answer yes, it was red. Yes? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please, 65 ter 5599. And page 285 of the English and 293 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We are turning now to the Mladic notebooks and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there has been a discussion on what to show, isn't it? The handwritten or the transcribed portion, is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, there has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, has that been resolved?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not sure to anyone's satisfaction, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because under those circumstances, I wonder why we couldn't show both the transcript and the original handwriting and that we consult the English version to the extent we need to do that, then you have everybody happy, isn't it? Well, I can't forecast who will be happy when, but -- if you take a solution-oriented approach, then you don't quarrel about whether to show A or B but to see whether you can show A and B so that -- and then of course the problem is that we don't have a translation, and due to our perfect e-court system, we can have on our other screen the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's acceptable to the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and also especially since it's very much date oriented, if we have the right document, but let's give it a try.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have page 285 and 293.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Which deals, Mr. Milovanovic, with Monday the 11th of May, 1992. And I want to pick up approximately where we left off with the issues we were discussing before the break with a few additional issues as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: One moment, please. We only have the page references for the typed copies, that's the only problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you then be clear on dates, then that might assist. So what we would then prefer to have -- oh, you have only the English transcribed pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. The English and the B/C/S, I beg your pardon, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have the B/C/S pages and if you have the originals then I wonder -- I don't know whether they go one on one or whether there's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The English is approximately one on one with the B/C/S typed, not always though, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and in the process in an effort to make them more easily used they have attempted to file the format of the handwritten notes to include some of the markings and to include the same pagination or roughly the same page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me now see -- the question is what to show to whom. You would like to see the original handwritten version, isn't it, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not that we would like to see the original handwritten version. We thought that Mr. Milovanovic would be aided by seeing the actual original handwritten page because there are certain ways that the notes were written that may also import some meaning into the actual text rather than the cold typewritten text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you have the page numbers ready, Mr. Jordash, for the English transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: For the English and the B/C/S typed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May, perhaps, I could just query one thing, there is a page number on the top of the English typed and there's also a page number on the bottom, I'm wondering if the page number on the top is a number which appeared in the Mladic originals which we might use to guide ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So let's start with one page and then I'll look at all the three versions and see whether we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The page -- the English typed Monday the 11th of May, 1992, Grmec command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page 290 at the top. But at the bottom, the English page 285 and the B/C/S page 293. This is the one I can see on the screen in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's get started on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The page, sir, I want to orientate you, Mr. Milovanovic, the 11th of May, and the Grmec command post, and I want to then turn to page 296 of the English and 304 of the B/C/S where Colonel Kovacevic is, or may be, speaking, according to the notes. This is the part of the same meeting according to the date, or certainly, this is the date which precedes the comments purportedly made by Colonel Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we could go to page 296 of the English and 304 of the B/C/S, please. I don't know if it's then possible to find the original handwritten and perhaps if we --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can be of some assistance. The number at the top of the page, Mr. Mladic numbered the pages in his notebooks so that 301 would correspond to the number page. If you indicate which notebook you are referring to, that page will be -- 301 will be the same page in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, it's 5599.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there we have the one, and that is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If I then refer to both the number at the top and the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would suggest that the numbering is relatively close. For example, the English translation page 301 appears on a page which at the bottom reads 296, so very close. If we try to orient ourselves very much on the numbering as we find it at the top of the pages in the original, which is reflected at least in the English, but let me have a look, I would say -- yes, 301, the numbering of the pages as written by the author do also appear both in the English version and in the -- and in the B/C/S version of the transcript. So I suggest that we work then -- you can choose your page if you know which page to choose, and then we'll have a look at the handwritten reference. For example, for page 301, that would be in the B/C/S transcript, is 304 out of 406. So it's all within a range of a couple of pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If you would read that entry just quickly, you probably have. Did you know Colonel Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was he responsible for weapons distribution, do you know, in the ten months before this entry, as he apparently appears to have said?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Ten months before this entry, I was in Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What about when you came into the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came into the Main Staff, Kovacevic was appointed deputy to General Djukic, who was assistant commander for logistical support.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you know what his previous history was in any way? Is there anything here which you would disagree with or have knowledge that would make you disagree with his comments?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Kovacevic for the first time that evening on the 11th of May and I knew about him only what General Mladic told us about each one of us, including General Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How long did Kovacevic maintain his position as assistant commander?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was deputy assistant commander. He was not assistant commander. He stayed there for a few months and then moved to another position to become minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was Djukic and -- well, was Djukic responsible for the distribution of weapons to the VRS during your time in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Djukic was responsible for procurement of weapons. I was responsible for distribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What did it mean to be responsible for distribution? What was the scheme in place?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To procure weapons for the army is one problem, you can do that by buying, borrowing, and distributing it means to give it to subordinate units. Chief of Staff knows best what to do, who needs more, who needs less, and he is the one who distributes the so-call strategic materials which are ammunition, which are weapons, fuel and food.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move forward, please to page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I inquire what Mr. Jordash intents on tendering these individual excerpts? It seems to the Prosecution that the Chamber, without the benefit of this in evidence, is left with a record that may cause some confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I agree. What we would hope do is tender the whole diary. Perhaps there will be a few pages which we wouldn't tender, but, generally speaking, will be the whole diary, rather than lots of little excerpts. We say the whole of the diaries are important because it demonstrates to Your Honours who was actually doing what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's irrespective of the expert report of Dr. Brown who we are waiting for.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, our position, as we've laid our previously, is that sections of the diary can be relied upon and some can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because you say I want the whole of it, virtually the whole of it to be admitted into evidence and then we'll later find out what parts can be relied upon and which parts cannot be relied upon. I mean, if you -- if it's in evidence, it's in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's the reason why I asked you for what purpose. Well, you say that we know who was doing what more or less, that suggests that you could rely on this to find out who was doing what and if you say at the same time that, well, some portions you may rely upon, others not, I'm a bit puzzled by what I'm supposed to do with it, and perhaps my colleagues as well. I see some nodding yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, in the same way that much of the evidence is admitted that a party will suggest at the final close of the case that it requires corroboration, some does and some doesn't, and that's our position in relation to the diaries. In relation to as I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest, for very practical reasons, the following procedure: You prepare a document, Mr. Jordash, which contains at least, I'm not saying exclusively, but at least all the pages we've looked at and what the witness testified about so that at least that is in evidence. If you say no, we need even more, then you can expand on that and perhaps it would be good to discuss it with Mr. Groome. Sometimes, for example, you would need other pages as well to have the proper time-frame. For example, I see that on page 301, for example, there's no date mentioned at all. We see that on the next page we have the 12th of May and the Assembly session. So the next page would be an indication that this, to the extent we can rely on it, preceded the 12th of May, what is written here and there's also some -- there's also some relation in substance because page 301 started for the Assembly which may well refer to what is about to happen the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I mean, I'm having difficulty explaining my position in front of the witness because we do say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the only thing I'm suggesting at this moment is that we, in one way or another, create a document which will be admitted so that we are not -- and that was the only concern Mr. Groome raised, I think, is that if the witness tells us about certain matters without having the underlying document in evidence, then it might be difficult to understand his testimony. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I don't believe it's necessary to even to decide how much of the diaries or notebooks are ultimately admitted into evidence. I'm just suggesting that there needs to be a proper record of what the witness was speaking about. May I suggest that every page of the document has the ERN number, this J000 number. If Mr. Jordash could simply include that reference in his question, then we will be able to reconstruct at a later time what it was the witness was making comments about, what specific entry the witness was speaking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For you just to have on the record the necessary information which would allow us to later reconstruct what we actually talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, then make full submissions on what should be admitted, what shouldn't be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, is that a good practical solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Except for the full submissions. We would want most of the diary in and we don't need to -- it's -- there are good reasons not to so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the only thing I think Mr. Groome is -- at this moment, is suggesting that we have a clear record of what we have looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then he suggested that to be done by reference to the ERN numbers which would, for the page we are looking at this moment, be J000-3072. At least if I'm -- that was the page 301 which is on my screen at this moment. I'll be happy to assist you. I'll read every number that appears on what I see on the screen, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not disagreeing with anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But Mr. Petrovic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe I may be allowed to contribute. In practical terms, I agree with -- you and Mr. Groome have suggested with regard to the clarity of the testimony of this witness. However, I would like to also support what Mr. Jordash has suggested, and that is that the diaries should be admitted in their entirety. Why? Because during our Defence case, certain parts of the diaries will be shown to some of the witnesses, some other parts will be tendered for admission from the bar table. In other words, there will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. If you want all of it in evidence, if Mr. Jordash wants most of it in evidence, I don't know what the position of Mr. Groome will be, sit together, say: This is what we would like, that's what we would like, make a short submission, OTP would like this to have in evidence, Stanisic Defence for this and this reason, 95 per cent of that, you everything. And then we have a kind of a bar table submission which is linked to what we have seen already in evidence, and at this moment then we'll not assign exhibit numbers but we'll just clearly put on the record what pages we looked at and I -- the page which is before us at this moment I read that out already. Next question or next portion, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have, please, page -- page 319 of the English, 327 of the B/C/S, and it's 324 at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 324, top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's the same diary -- notebook, I beg your pardon, 5599. It's an entry that relates to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are looking at this moment at J000-3095.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the date to orient yourself, Mr. Milovanovic, is the 14th of May, 1992. And there's a list there, as you can see, of items which were sent to the Territorial Defence of Bosnia from the Federal Secretariat of the National Defence. Were you aware of these deliveries from the federal secretariat of the national defence?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was the federal secretariat of national defence not making regular supplies to the Bosnian Territorial Defence around this time?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Wouldn't you know that in your position at the Main Staff, especially given your particular tasks concerning supplies?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, sir, the handwriting doesn't tell me that it was sent from the federal secretariat of the national defence. I can't see that from the handwriting. I can see it in the English version. Second of all, on the 14th of May, the -- in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were two Territorial Defence troops. The first one was of the Muslim and Croatian coalition and the Territorial Defence of the Republika Srpska army which became part of the Republika Srpska army. I don't know who this was sent to because at that time negotiations were underway between Alija Izetbegovic on the one side and the General Staff of the SFRY, or rather, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the other hand. And the negotiations were about releasing recruits and officers from many barracks in the Sarajevo garrison in exchange for infantry weapons. And I know that the chief of the General Staff of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, General Panic, asked for me to let everything go to Sarajevo once it arrived on the Drina River. He wanted to make sure that the soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska would not requisition that. I don't know when Mladic wrote that. I don't know when. You said that it was on the 14th, and I don't have any reason not to believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What does the title on the left-hand screen say? Is that different or could you just read it? Right at the top of the screen on the left.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Sent to the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina." At that time we already bore the title the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was our official title.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on to page 344 of the English, 352 of the B/C/S, and 349 at the top of the page and it's J000-3120.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We can see there that Mladic has taken a number down there, the Ministry for Serbs outside of Serbia. Did you have dealings with the Ministry for Serbs Outside Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I've never heard of that ministry before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You can't cast light then on why Mladic would take down this number?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What number?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The number under the title "Ministry for Serbs outside of Serbia," or the various numbers which seem to relate to that heading, including a fax number.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This person Gojko Djogo, his name is at the top. I know that he was a poet or something of the kind. Simo Djuretic, I don't have a clue who he was. And I know that at that time there were attempts, failed attempts to establish a committee in Belgrade headed by the retired general, Blagoje Adzic. And that committee should have mediated their exchange of weapons between Republika Srpska and Republic of Yugoslavia or Serbia. In the Republika Srpska, we inherited big military companies like Adzic and others. I told you how we were supplied with ammunition. In Republika Srpska we made shells and then we sent them off to the Republic of Serbia where they would be filled with charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, we are looking at this moment at page 0668-3168. Please proceed. No, I'm now a bit confused, as a matter of fact. Mr. Groome, I see a number now in -- in e-court which is J000-3120. At the same time, I find a version in e-court where this number does not appear on that same spot. However, where another number appears, but this is a black and white copy, perhaps that's the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can just assist the Chamber. The government of Serbia originally provided the Office of the Prosecutor with a scanned version that they had created and that is the other number. When the Prosecution received the original books, took the decision to re-scan them and that is the original with the red J number, and the J prefix has only been used for the material recovered from General Mladic's home. So it may even be sufficient for the Chamber to say J number 3120 but that will clearly indicate the page of the original document and not a previous scan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that, and that's the one because in e-court there are two originals, apparently. That's the one you scanned and which bears the J000 numbers and the other numbers, apparently then, are the previously-sent scanned copies by the Republic of Serbia is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I'm sorry for creating the confusion, but two originals is always confusing me a bit. But the matter is clear now. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You made reference then to a process whereby ammunition was being sent to Republic of Serbia to be filled with charges. How long did that go on for?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That went on throughout the entire war, but let me correct myself with regard to my previous answer. May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me if I knew anything about the Ministry for Serbs Outside Serbia. When the SFRY broke up, the ministry of Serbs for Serbs in diaspora was set up in the Republic of Serbia. And that ministry still exists in Serbia, I believe. That ministry rallies around itself the entire Serbian diaspora, not only those in Bosnia-Herzegovina or Croatia, but in the United States of America, Australia and further afield, and that ministry still exists and functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know that in July of 1991, Bogdanovic, previous minister of the interior, took over as the minister of that organisation?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's hard for me to remember the names of all the ministers in Republika Srpska, let alone Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What, then, in your mind or from your knowledge, did the minister of -- or Ministry of Serbs for Serbs outside of Serbia do in relation to the VRS? What might that connection have been with Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They may have sought links with General Mladic because those Serbs created their associations in America and Australia and donated money to the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's move to 65 ter 5600 and page 2 of the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is the beginning of Mladic's -- a Mladic notebook which begins at the 31st of May, 1992. Was it -- when you see the page, have a look at the page, what -- was it, as far as you know, Mladic's practice to put important numbers, telephone numbers at the beginning of his notebooks?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was common practice of all officers. Just after the cover page there are, I believe, 12 pages designed for you to enter important telephone numbers and other such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And these would be numbers which would be important, presumably, to the author of a particular notebook, these are the numbers that he would be in contact with directly? Was that the general practice?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when you met somebody, when you talk to somebody, when you became friends or wanted to maintain business relations with them, we normally asked them for their telephone numbers and we would enter those numbers into the notebook. That was common practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we are looking at page J000-3178.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Let's move forward, past through the telephone numbers to page 36 of the English and 36 of the B/C/S, and the entry is the 31st of May, 1992. And then let's just, having orientated ourselves, let's move on to page 37 -- sorry, 38 of the English and 38 of the B/C/S and 37 at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And we can see that Mladic is apparently at Jahorina and having a meeting with the leadership of the Serbian Republic of the BH. It's a long time --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the original is J000-3213.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's a long time ago. Do you recall if you were present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's move forward to page 41 of the English and 41 of the B/C/S and 40 at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it looks as though Karadzic may still be speaking. And at the top there is a comment there, "We cannot use aircraft any longer except in extreme necessity." And then down below reference to Mauzer, who we were talking about earlier. Are you able to comment on the apparent assertion by Karadzic or someone who was at that meeting that aircraft could not any longer be used except in extreme necessity.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of comment you want me to make. I don't want to mention the spare wheel on that red car.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, was it the case that in May you saw that the VRS aircraft or aircraft in VRS territory could no longer be used except in extreme necessity?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May? No. Discussions on air force started in October in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In relation to Mauzer, do you confirm that there was discussions in the Main Staff and upwards towards Karadzic concerning Mauzer and the need to subordinate him in May?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
