utterances.text: May and June were the month when we discussed paramilitaries and when we started a process to subordinate them under the command of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And at this point in time had Mauzer been receiving his supplies from the JNA supplies?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. It was only when he became our member, when he was subordinated to us that he started receiving supplies from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Where was he getting them before that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't really know where paramilitaries got their supplies from.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Wasn't the SDS distributing them to the likes of Mauzer at this point before the commencement of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every political party, I mean, the major stronger political parties, had its own paramilitary of sorts and they provided the funding, and if you have the money, it's not difficult to buy weapons and ammunition. I believe the SDS funded Mauzer, although Mauzer himself, I believe, had his own political party. I don't know who they were relying on, but they were not relying on anyone in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to say in relation - now you've seen this diary entry - when it was that the VRS started to give Mauzer supplies?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you the date. I can tell you the time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the month of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think I said the number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We looked at J000-3216.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go to page 60 of the English and B/C/S and 59 at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And we are at the same meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Should be 59 at the top and 60 at the bottom, please, of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the comment which goes: "Send Major Radojcic from the Sarajevo training centre to Ozren." What was the Sarajevo training centre in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the original, it doesn't say training centre, it says school centre. And a school centre for mechanised armour units was located --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, could you please slow down a bit when you are speaking and perhaps I could invite you to repeat your answer where you said: "In the original, it doesn't say training centre, it says school centre," and then you explained that "the school centre for," and could you please repeat from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a school centre for the training of NCOs officers and reserves officers in tank crews in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know why the major was sent to Ozren?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to confirm whether he, in fact, was sent to Ozren?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen him in Ozren. And I went there more than once.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was there a VRS training centre there?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At Ozren there was a combat unit, an operative group called Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And who were they subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were part of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And who was the commander, please?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was the operative group, the combat unit organising training at Ozren?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Training centres of the VRS were in Banja Luka, Bijeljina, and Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The training centre in Banja Luka, how big was that, please? How many men was it training, for example, a week or a month?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many but it was never the same number. It depended on the population base from which recruitment was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When was that set up, please?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was established right at the beginning of the war when we received the first contingent of recruits in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And how long did it continue to operate, please?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic training of recruits in those centres lasted for three or three and a half months, after which they went on to the second stage of their training in combat units, but they could not be used in combat before having been in the army for eight months.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can you give us a sense of how big this operation was, how many personnel were involved in this training centre?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you how many people were working there, but I know that these training centres were parts of corps: One in Banja Luka was part of the 1st Krajina Corps; the one in Bijeljina belonged to the Eastern Bosnia Corps; and another in Bileca belonged to the Herzegovina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And how significant were these training centres for the work of the VRS? Did most personnel who were with the VRS at this point go through these training centres?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those that were the generation of 1972. I don't know what the growth was during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, what does that mean, "those that were the generation of 1972"? Could you just explain that answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, recruitment covers men aged 18. They usually called up when they turn 18 and as a young man turned 18, they were sent to one of these centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what about those paramilitary groups or TO units who had been subordinated to the VRS from May of 1992 onwards? Did they go through these training centres? Were they expected to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because children did not join paramilitary units. It was military conscripts who failed to respond to the mobilisation in Republika Srpska that was announced on the 21st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: As far as you were aware, were there any other training centres in Banja Luka at the time that the VRS was operating their training centre?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean centres for the paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Any training centre, I mean, other than the VRS training centre?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the territory of Republika Srpska there was only one centre, to the best of my knowledge, that was kept in Dragan centre in Divic near Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And how long did that last?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Dragan operated first in the area of the Knin Krajina, then when the Vance Plan was signed for the stabilisation of relations, or rather, the cessation of hostilities in Croatia, this self-styled captain no longer could find any place for himself in Krajina, and not wanting to go to Serbia or back to Australia where he had come from, he stopped at the border at the Divic and started rallying some specialists whom he trained himself, but with this order of the 28th of June we broke up his group.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll come to Dragan in a minute, but just how long did this training centre exist? That's all I want to know for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it existed for more than a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on. I will return to Dragan shortly because he does make an appearance in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's move now to page 151 of the English and -- sorry, 151 of the English and 149 of the B/C/S, and it's 148 at the top of the page. And the original is J000-3322.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And so you can orientate yourself, perhaps we need to go back one page, and the date we are looking at is an entry on the 11th of June which is at page 146 of the English and 144 of the B/C/S. And we have an entry there which is headed "Bijeljina," and then if we go over the page we have the reference again to Mauzer, self-proclaimed major, got some of Arkan's decorations or others, has a hold over half the municipal Presidency in Bijeljina, et cetera. The brain behind the whole team is Jesaric, connected through business and relatives. His unit is in the barracks in Bijeljina. He made Dencic appoint him to the duty of commander for counter-intelligence affairs. Were you aware of these details? Were they accurate, as far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me to be able to speak about it, you have to give me the time-frame or the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think it's the -- yes, it's Thursday, the 11th of June.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this about Mauzer in that period: When General Mladic spoke to him, and this is what Mladic told me, Mauzer stripped his own insignia of rank off and he wanted to return them to General Mladic because he had not received them from the VRS, which he was joining. Mladic took those insignia and then returned them to Mauzer and said: From now on you are a soldier of the VRS. So I don't know whether he was a self-styled major or he actually got that rank from someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was he located in the barracks in Bijeljina at this point in time along with VRS personnel?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where he was based because I was not in touch with him. I know that he set up that brigade himself before the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, what he had done with that brigade and where before we arrived, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How big was the VRS presence in the barracks in Bijeljina at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know their strength. I know there were two or three brigades from the Eastern Bosnia Corps at all times. It was a large barracks and it was probably used for R & R, rest and recreation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How did the brigades that were there receive their supplies? Was there a logistics base in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a logistical base in Bijeljina but it was attached to the Main Staff, not to the Eastern Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did the Eastern Bosnia Corps receive logistics through the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know why Mladic hadn't subordinated Mauzer before June, in the month of May, for example?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already spoke about that, he simply didn't have enough time. These paramilitary commanders first needed to be spoken to, then they had to be given time to make their decision, and then the order came down in June. I don't know. Maybe it happened in May, but I know that he was the first one that Mladic spoke to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move to page 245 of the English and 243 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think that we have a full record yet. I think the page where who again was sent to Ozren, it was Colonel -- Major -- you had forgotten to read the page number of that one. That was J000-3235.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the next one you read. And we are now moving to?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: To page 245 of the English and 243 of the B/C/S, with 242 at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we are now looking at J000-3416.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Before I ask you a question about that, could I just ask you who is Dencic, Mr. Milovanovic? There I'm referring to the earlier entry where Mladic apparently writes that Mauzer made Dencic -- appointed him to the duty of commander for counter-intelligence affairs. Do you know who Dencic is or was?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Dencic, I forget his first name, was assistant for logistics in the 11th JNA corps in Tuzla. With the decision to withdraw the JNA, the corps commander - I forget his name as well but I know he died recently - left Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Dencic, the assistant for logistics, stood in for the commander of the Eastern Bosnia Corps for awhile. He was a man who did not do very well as corps commander, and we had to replace him very quickly. He was the one, actually, who gave Captain Dragan approval for setting up that training centre in Divic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Against the command of his commander?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whose commander you mean, Dencic's commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who was Dencic's commander at the time Dencic gave Captain Dragan approval to set up the training centre?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dencic was acting commander of the Eastern Bosnia Corps, and his superior was supreme commander Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to the entry on the screen, J000-3416. And I'm interested in the reference to the training centre Captain 1st Class Markovic. Are you able to cast any light on what that might be a reference to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which Markovic that is because I know dozens of Markovics in the VRS ranging from lieutenants to colonels, so I can't tell you anything. I can't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to connect training centre with Zvornik? Is there any connection there?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, sir, I can only give you my inferences and my opinions. I don't think I should be doing that as a witness though. There was a Markovic in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, if all you can do is give your opinion -- if you've got facts that might help the Court, please give them, but otherwise we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to 215 of the English, 213 of the B/C/S, and 212 at the top of the page. And it's J000-3386.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And a meeting apparently with the minister of defence, Colonel Subotic. What was his precise role at this point in time? What did it involve being the minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Bogdan Subotic was the first defence minister of Republika Srpska. I know more about what is written here. We found out that in the bauxite mine in Milici, around Milici, there was some sort of embezzlement or looting or something, and President Karadzic sent Subotic as defence minister to find out what it was all about, to inquire. Subotic went there, and after that he informed General Mladic about the general situation in Milici. Since this was on the 20th June, the major problem for the army in Milici was this: The president of municipality of Milici was at the same time director manager of the bauxite mine and he refused to carry out the mobilisation in Milici, the mobilisation that was proclaimed on the 21st of May. What made things worse, he was also president of the Executive Board of the SDS, and in this -- on this party ladder he was man number two in the Serbian Democratic Party and he refused to carry out the mobilisation, and that's why the president sent the defence minister to inquire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm happy to pause there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we resume at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We were talking about Subotic and the situation in Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if -- this is J000-3387. And Mladic apparently writes that a police officer from Zvornik was present who pointed out the problem of the training centre formed by Captain Dragan in Divic village near Zvornik, these men broken loose from any command. Do you know whose command they broke loose from at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to Captain Dragan and what he said to General Mladic, but this is the first time I saw that Captain Dragan met up with Mladic. I saw it from the materials that you gave me yesterday. I didn't know about that. Captain Dragan dreaded [as interpreted] around himself some people who didn't want to join the army, as a matter of fact, either in Serbia or in the Republic of Serbian Krajina while he was there, or when he came to Republika Srpska. Those were usually lads with a lot of problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but the entry seems to suggest he was under a command at one point. Are you able to cast any light on that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't cast any light on that. What I've just told you is something that I saw in your materials, actually. I know that Dencic took him under his wing. He was the commander of the Eastern Bosnia Corps and he allowed him to set up that training centre in Divic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And who was he training under that authority?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those lads that he rallied around himself, and I don't know how he did that. When I arrived at that centre for the first time with an intention to dismantle it, I found some 20 lads there. They were idle. They didn't do anything. Captain Dragan was not there. And I arrived because General Mladic had ordered me to find a way to get rid of Captain Dragan, and I believe that I've already told you how that came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So do I have this accurately, that as far as you are aware that Captain Dragan trained some lads and before they actually did anything they were removed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He stayed in Divic for a month or a month and a half, as I've already told you. He was never in any action with them because I was responsible for eliminating him and this is what I did. I gave him a task knowing that he was not capable of carrying that task out. We was stringing me along for some four days and then we agreed to meet up in Milici. Allegedly he wanted me to personally give him that task verbally. I arrived in Milici. He was not there. I was told that he had left for Zvornik 10 minutes before that. Then I went to Zvornik, to the command of the Zvornik Brigade, and I was told there that 10 minutes before I arrived he left for Divic. My security chief was against us going back to Divic. He was afraid that he would be ambushed. Still, we went there. Dragan wasn't there. He had fled to Belgrade in the meantime, and then I said to those lads: Collect your things and leave. The lads left. The training centre was dismantled. Captain Dragan never showed up there after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I seek clarification of one of the answers. You said a minute ago that: "According to Captain Dragan and what he said to General Mladic, but this is the first time I saw that Captain Dragan met up with Mladic. I saw it from the materials that you gave me yesterday ..." That is an unclear reference for us because we have not gone through all the materials, but it is not on the page we have just looked at, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps I can take Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know whether you find it of any importance, but I just wanted to make clear that it's a reference to a source which is unknown to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll take Your Honours to it. Page 264 of the English and 262 of the B/C/S. 261 at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It seems to be attached to a date, the 30th of June, 1992, which is at page 246 of the English and 244 of the B/C/S. Now, we are looking at the screen at J000-3435. We see there reference halfway down the page meeting with Dragan at his request. And then reading further down the page we have, it seems -- well, we have an entry which says: "I met Dragan when Colonel Ilic came," and this may be Deputy Mijatovic stating this, "we both said what was good. The blockade of the municipality and busting into the building with weapons is something that cannot be tolerated. Nothing could be taken from Divic to be placed in the war reserves depot as war booty." Now, was that a reference to Dragan or his men taking items and keeping them at Divic rather than -- as personal properties rather than as war booty?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I certainly am.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me answer the Presiding Judge's question. Mladic never told me that he had met up with Captain Dragan. He arrived back one evening and the only thing he told me was find a way to eliminate Captain Dragan from Republika Srpska, and I found a way, and I told you how I did it. This is the first time that I realised that General Mladic had ever met up with Captain Dragan. And as for the things that Mladic found in Divic, I didn't find them myself. I saw in your materials that Mijatovic had told Mladic that Captain Dragan was nothing but a common thief and he had even stormed a Serbian municipality and blockaded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You were unaware of that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, at the bottom of the page it says: "Zuca and Crni would even burst," and we go over the page, "into the surgical theatre during operations." Was Zuca and Crni working hand in hand with Dragan -- or were they working hand in hand with Dragan?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I believe that the two were two separate organisations. From time to time Crni would appear at Zuca's. I don't know what Crni had or what he did. I believe that he was an individual who operated on his own, a maverick. I heard of him during the war. I believe that he was removed together with Zuca. I know that Zuca was convicted to a prison sentence of 15 years and that he died in the Sremska Mitrovica prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How many men did Crni have at this point, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was he doing?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I ever saw Crni was some time in the summer of 1992. I believe that it was either in July or in August. He arrived at Mladic's office. He arrived from Herzegovina. Mladic talked to him and then he called me from the place where he was billeted and he told me: A man is going to come to your office, can you listen to him for awhile and then tell me what you think? And then give him a helicopter tomorrow to transfer him and another man, Captain Janic to Herzegovina. And that person indeed came. He told me how he, on his own, had taken the repeater over from Muslim on Leutar [phoen] mountain, the same repeater that the Muslims had taken in 1993. The Herzegovina Corps tried to restore possession of that repeater for awhile, that was the hub of our communication, and that happened. And Crni bragged that it was owing to him. What he was doing in Herzegovina, I don't know. Whether him and Captain Dragan co-operated, I don't know. I don't know who controlled him, whether he was under anybody's supervision, whether he had any men under him. I don't even know his real name. I don't know his first name or his last name, I don't know who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Is there any reason why you were not aware of the size of his group? Does that suggest anything to you about the size of his group or the activities of his group?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. As I've already told you, I believe that he was a maverick, an individual who operated on his own. A lonely wolf.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's what I'm suggesting. You don't know that he was subordinated within the JNA or the VRS and you don't know anything about the size of his group, does that suggest that he was insignificant in terms of war operations or in terms of criminality?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already told you, I don't know anything about him. When Mladic sent him to my office and when I talked to him, he told me that he prevented the assassination of the commander of the Herzegovina Corps. There was a skirmish between the commanders security detail or the security detail of a brigade and the brigade's name was Ante Boro. His security detail conflicted with General Grubic's security detail. One man was dead as a result of that, and Crni bragged that he was the one who managed to protect General Grubic, but it never occurred to me later to check it with the general himself. So as I've already told you, I don't know who that man was. I only saw him once and that's the long and the short of the whole story.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go back, please, in the diary to -- still sticking with 65 ter 5600, page 117 of the English and 116 of the B/C/S. Sorry, I should have said the number at the top of the page which is 115. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is -- before I start that, this is J000-3289 and the title is: "The Monday, the 8th of June request of the General Staff of the Army of the FRY." And it concerns co-ordination groups, groups which purportedly co-ordinating such things as technical administration, quartermaster administration, air force and anti-aircraft defence. Do you know anything about these co-ordination groups and what their significance, if any, was to Mladic and the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let's look at the title. I don't know whether these are requests by the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia upon the Army of Republika Srpska or whether it is Mladic's request upon the General Staff of the Federal Army of Yugoslavia. It's very difficult to understand. However, when it comes to that group, I know about that group. I started answering your question about the ministry for services outside of Serbia. I know that the retired General Adzic wanted to set up a group. They would co-operate amongst themselves and they would deal with the production of ammunition. Moreover, we had a lot of refugees, military conscripts who were in Serbia. It would have been a whole corps strong of deserters in Serbia. As far as I know, General Djukic was supposed to join that group together with Mico Grubor, the head of personnel in the Army of Republika Srpska. I also know that that group never really took off the ground. In any case, General Adzic never took the lead because there was a ban on his entering the General Staff of the Republic of Serbia for some reason. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just have a moment. Let's go, can we, please, 230 of the English, 228 of the B/C/S and 227 at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is an entry which relates to June the 24th, 1992, and it is a meeting of the collegium of the Main Staff of the Army of the RS. I beg your pardon, it's a briefing of Colonel Zivanovic at 1330 hours at page 228 of the English and 226 of the B/C/S. Have you read these entries concerning Skelani and the Bajina Basta dam and the torching of Serbian villages?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did you agree with its contents, from your own personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what Colonel Zivanovic reported to General Mladic because Mladic had sent him to Eastern Bosnia, that is to say Skelani, to see what the situation was there. Then Colonel Zivanovic was acting as chief of artillery of the Main Staff, and when he returned, he told this sorry. I personally did not agree with that account of Colonel Zivanovic because he glorified that battalion and we had a lot of problems with it. First of all, people had abandoned the newly-established municipality of Skelani. They ran away across the Drina, across Bajina Basta to Serbia, so we had to send a battalion from the 1st Krajina Corps to deal with it and they did so within 24 hours. Colonel Zivanovic sang and ode of praise to that battalion and the situation was not really like he depicted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What about the torching of the Muslim villages, was that accurate or not? I beg your pardon, torching of the Serbian villages?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was true. In one of my appearances here, I don't know whether it was in this case or another, I said that by 14 February 1993, that's to say between April 1992 until 14 February 1993, around 156 Serbian villages and hamlets had been destroyed, looted and burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That was in this trial so we don't need to go over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to instead to page 246 of the English and 244 of the B/C/S, and 243 at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, the previous page you located in time on the 24th of June, whereas I see the 24th of June appearing on page 217 at the top, or is it 219, whereas half a page before the briefing starts it seems to say the 25th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: My mistake. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is now J000-3417 and it's a meeting, it seems, with Mladic and representatives of the Zvornik municipality. And we can see the list of those present. Can we move then to page 247 of the English and 245 of the B/C/S, and 244 at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And there's an entry there with Novak Tokanovic, commander of, it seems, the Sekovici detachment, part of the Birac Brigade, speaking about a unit called the guard operating under the JNA. Do you know which unit Tokanovic is referring to or appears to be referring to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand point this Tokanovic was the commander. He was a commissioner of the SDS for the municipality of Sekovici. I know there was a period where there was some sort of ruckus in Sekovici, somebody had formed a paramilitary unit, but it was not given the status of a military unit but a police unit, and the commander of the Milici Brigade, Andric Svetozar, refused to accept that unit into his brigade. That caused a conflict between the municipal authorities and the brigade command and Mladic went there to sort it out. I believe that meeting was held in Vlasenica with the local municipal presidents of Milici, Sekovici, Vlasenica and I don't know who else was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You can see the reference to the guard operating under the JNA. Who might that have been? Are you able to explain that? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, what date are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The date on the screen now, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we are talking about the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, the date isn't on the screen but it's the 30th of June. And there's a reference there, if you can see it, to the guard operating under the JNA, according to Tokanovic. The question is: Do you know who that might be?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 30th June which year?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It couldn't have been the JNA because the JNA had left Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 20th of May, 1992. I think rather --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm bit puzzled by your question. You are referring to the guard and then you ask who that may be, and from the context it seems that it's a unit and so what -- I always refer -- who for me is a person that -- but perhaps that's my lack of understanding of the English language. Say Mr. X, who is that; and I would say the unit, what is it, or not who is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll make myself clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The entry says: "Before the arrival of the army, we had one unit that was called the guard. It operated under the JNA." Do you know anything about that unit, Mr. Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's move on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to page 263 of the English, 261 of the B/C/S, and 260 at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's the same meeting we were looking at, the meeting of the representatives in Zvornik. And I'm interested in the comment made by Mladic, it seems, or the statement written down that "one called Crni gave your name as a reference." It looks as though Jokic told Mladic that. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Jokic. I told you before how I met Crni, Mladic had sent him to me, and Crni must have dropped Mladic's name when he was seeing Captain Jokic. I don't know whether he referred to Mladic or not but it's likely that he did because Mladic had sent him to me and he must have -- or he could have sent him to Jokic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's J-- I can't see the number, actually, on that. J000-3434. Let's move on to 316 of the English, 314 of the B/C/S and the top of the page is 313. It's an entry for the Sunday, 12th of July, 1992. Now, it's a bit unclear what this is, in the sense it's a meeting or whatever, but it seems as though Major-General Gvero is there, and the president of Bileca municipality is present at some point. That's, Your Honours 317 of the English and B/C/S, 315. And I'm interested in page 318 of the English and 316 of the B/C/S, and the top of the page is 315. And the comment there situation in -- this is a third of the way down the page: "Situation in Gacko municipality fine. Berkovici municipality says there's disorder in the army - Arkan's Men who want to loot and want the army to equip them before going into battle. Wants the aim of the war in Herzegovina defined."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Arkan seeking for the VRS to equip him in this municipality?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was 12 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan had been expelled by then from the territory of Republika Srpska. It's possible, however, that a smaller group of his had gone to Herzegovina because they had not found a place for themselves in Eastern Bosnia, and I remember this, General Mladic sent Gvero as his assistant for moral guidance to Herzegovina to talk all or most of the situations there and size-up the situation, especially from the viewpoint of the attitude of the civilian authorities towards the army. I have no other comment to make on this. This is Gvero's report to Mladic. However, on the previous page, I just noticed at the bottom of the page a different pencil. Could I also see it again to compare the handwriting? I want to see if it's the same handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go back, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there was a page where I saw writing in blue. There it is. Sunday, 12 July. It's St. Peter's day, the Serbian holiday. Same handwriting but I can't understand -- maybe he ran out of ink and changed pens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Should we move on? Is that all you wanted to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have anything to say about this but I do have a comment on the material given me yesterday. An initial of General Mladic was copied mistakenly. Almost everywhere it's BM, whereas it should be RM for Ratko Mladic because he wrote the letter B in a very specific way as an open 8, so probably the person transcribing it misunderstood. That's the way Mladic wrote R. Everywhere I saw it was written BM, and in his work notebook, Mladic never put his initials. Or maybe those were the initials of somebody who transcribed it or copied it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't think there's going to be any dispute about this, that's Mladic's wife who signed the document when they were -- when they appeared -- when they were found at the apartment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bosa Mladic. Then it's my mistake. I thought it was Mladic's initial.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just for your information, she signed every page before the documents were handed over to the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I reviewed 23 of Mladic's notebooks, some in The Hague, some in Banja Luka. Only in three of them did I find that Bosa put page numbers in green felt tip pen and on the back of these three notebooks she wrote that she, Bosa Mladic, reviewed and put page numbers on the pages 1 to 400 and the actual pages begin with number 13. That's the beginning of the actual writing space. The first 12 pages are filled with office phone numbers, calendars, agenda, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on. Perhaps that's to be resolved at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to page 355 of the English, 353 of the B/C/S, 353 at the top of the page. It's entry 15th of July, 1992, and it's a briefing of the organs of command of the Main Staff of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And it's J000-3527.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you present during this briefing?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant to say that the end of this examination what I reviewed last night is one and a half of these binders. I never found my name or my title anywhere. Whereas not a single briefing at the Main Staff could have gone on without me because I'm the person who analysed combat activities, evaluated the situation, and made proposals to the commander. In my prior review of some notebooks, I found my name, or rather, a reference to me in the letters NS, which stands for Chief of Staff. However, in what I reviewed yesterday, I did not come across my name anywhere. Even here it begins with the General Tolimir, chief of security and intelligence, or perhaps we'll come across Petar Salapura, the first man in intelligence, followed by Chief of Staff or the operative officer, if there is no Chief of Staff, but I didn't even find Miletic here who briefs the commander about the military situation or the condition in the VRS. And after a everyone has spoken, the Chief of Staff takes the floor again and makes a proposal to the Commander-in-Chief about employment of the army. But that whole segment is missing as if I was nowhere there in the army. In the last half of 1992, I was there all the time. I never moved out of that hutment because that's the time when the army was being established. I was only absent for 24 hours on the 2nd of August to visit my mother in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, before I give an opportunity to Mr. Groome, you said it was an entry of the 15th of July, where it rather clearly says the 20th of July, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just above.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, complete misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Milovanovic on several occasions now has made some observations about the materials that he reviewed last night, yet there is to clear record of what it was that he was given. Could I ask that Mr. Jordash be given an opportunity at the beginning of tomorrow's session to put on the record what it was that General Milovanovic was given, either orally or perhaps even a written demonstrative exhibit that is an index of the materials that General Milovanovic was asked to review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I will draft something and file it with Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we'll then have a look at it. At the same time I think one of the last answers of Mr. -- of the witness was approximately one page, and that all answering the question: Were you present during the briefing? Now, it could be that you have hidden your search for all this information in this question, but I really wonder whether you are interested in it, and if so, then I would have put a different question perhaps then to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to know if he was presents, I didn't expect him to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... yes, but then you should interrupt him and say: Were you present? Not, if not then put a next question to the witness instead of let him go a full page, unless it was all exactly what you were --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, I thought Your Honours might be interested in any reflection that the witness had about the authenticity of the diary. Notebook, I mean. But I can move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, about the name and the way in which RM or BM was written, that's clear, but that's whether all that -- okay. I leave it to you, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I take Your Honour's point and I'll step in earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 20th of July, 1992. Let's go to the next page, and I want to try to move swiftly because I'm running out of time, Mr. Milovanovic. So try to focus your answers, if you would. There's reference there to NATO stepping up reconnaissance activities. Did they step up reconnaissance activities around July of 1992 to prevent the VRS from using aircraft within Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: NATO reconnaissance sorties did start but I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did it prevent you using aircraft within Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I've already told you, our air force was grounded in October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware through your own reconnaissance what air -- who was in the air-space over Bosnia? Which aircraft were using the air-space in VRS territory?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who they were. I only know that it wasn't Iceland because Iceland does not have an armed force and they are still NATO member state.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's move on, perhaps we are both getting tired.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to page 357 of the English and 355 of the B/C/S. 355 at the top of the page. And it's the same meeting and it's a comments by Colonel Lukic: "There are 110 recruits at the training centre, 295 in Bileca. They are to complete their training on the 30th of July."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Colonel Lukic was head of personnel and he took charge of recruitment and the deployment of soldiers and officers. I personally brought them over from Nis to join the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was the training as described in this notebook?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already told you, we had three training centres in Banja Luka, Bijeljina and Bileca, as you can see there's training in Bileca, you asked me about the number of recruits, I didn't know, but it says here 295, that was the first generation of recruits that we recruited to serve in our army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that around this time and throughout 1992 training and the lack thereof was a problem for the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a shortage of recruits and that was a problem. As I've already told you, in Serbia there was a corps strong of deserters. The children who were growing up at that time, those were the children of parents who could not leave Bosnia and Herzegovina. Everybody else did. And also, we had the problem with military conscripts who remained in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina because their specialties did not meet the demands of the Army of Republika Srpska. We had the biggest number of infantry men so we had to retrain them to become artillery men, to become members of our air force, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yeah. And the problem I'm suggesting that there was not just the number of recruits but the amount of training that was being administered which led to extensive damage, for example, of combat equipment because the training wasn't adequate; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a fair description. That's why we had an obligatory military service of 8 months plus 8 months, which means that while they were in training for 8 months they could not be used in combat. After that they could be deployed and used in combat. Their service was not interrupted so as to allow them to be mobilised. Their service was continuous which means that they had to stay in the army for 16 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And a lack of training or a lack of adequate training meant that there were a disproportionate number of deaths and wounded in the VRS; is that also fair?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This should be correct but it wasn't. As I've already told you several times, the first 8 months of training meant that recruits were not used in combat. And this was precisely with a view to reducing our casualties. We did not want untrained men to die in vain.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But that is what happened, though, in 1992, isn't it? Men were dying in vain because the training wasn't adequate? I can take you, if you want, to your VRS combat 1992 report.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you think this is necessary, be my guest. Show it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's only necessary if you don't remember what is in it, or you don't remember this as being a problem within the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are casualties in every war. The task of the command cadre is to reduce those losses to a minimum. It would have been a crime to use a new recruit and let him die because he was not well trained, and at the same time the enemy was better trained than was able to locate such an untrained soldier and kill him. That would have been a crime.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all unnecessary microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's return to that tomorrow then and I won't delay things now by finding the reference but we'll return to that. Let's move on. Page 377 of the English and 375 of the B/C/S and 375 at the top of the page. And we've just looked at J000-3529.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see 549.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's what we now have on the screen, J000-3549. And this is an entry dated the 27th of July, 1992, and it's at page 373 of the English and 371 of the B/C/S, and it talks with Minister of the Interior, Mr. Mico Stanisic and the deputy minister of the government, Mr. Trbojevic. And we see there -- perhaps we go back one page so we can see how we get to this page. Gavrilo Kukic, Crni from Bileca. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the one and the same Crni of whom I spoke at length, but I didn't know what his name really was, now I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: He is the Crni who was refusing to subordinate himself and then was sent by Mladic somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that that is him because he also told me that together with four lads he managed to restore the possession of the repeater.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, 377, let's go back to the next page, where he appears to speak about some Red Berets, seven or eight of them are working for them, all they care about is stealing a car. Are they the, from what you can see then -- the men you were referring to under Crni?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The question is: Did that Crni refer to his group as the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't mention them to me. He just mentioned those four lads and I don't know whether they were Red Berets. He just said four lads. He did not specify who they were, whether they were civilians or soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's move on to 65 ter 5601, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And again this notebook starts off, as we'll see, with a whole range of numbers, telephone numbers of, it seems, Mladic's contacts at that point in time, and the diary starts at the 2nd of August, 1992. Could we go, please, to page --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we go please to page 22 of the English and B/C/S and 21 at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it's is a meeting on Sunday the 2nd of August, 1992, with the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of BH. And Karadzic appears to be there and speaking, and he says, or so it appears, "There are strong autonomous tendencies present in Banja Luka." And then if we just stay there for a moment, that's J000-2197. Then if we go across the page to the next page: "The Red Berets must be put under control right away. Lieutenant-Colonel Sajic has established a group of brigades that constitute an autonomist army." Is that something that you are aware of, Mr. Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already told you, on that day I was in Vranje. However, as for that story about the autonomous movement, I learned all that perhaps a day or two later. The man whose name you mentioned and in the meantime I've forgotten, did you say Sajic? I believe someone from the 1st Krajina Corps came to the Main Staff, I can't remember who it was, and he told us that Karadzic's idea was to create one state comprising of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the Republika Srpska, and to that effect a declaration was passed under the name of Prijedor declaration or something like that. However, at the outset it didn't make too much sense or perhaps Karadzic was afraid that the world would not accept that solution. That is why people from the two Krajinas, the Bosnian Krajina from the river Zoklena [phoen] to the Una and the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, meaning the Krajina of Knin, Kordun, Banija, Western Slavonia decided that a Krajina state would be created from those provinces or states, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, I just want to focus on Red Berets. Could you get to that point, please, if you know anything about them?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything. My only encounter with the Red Berets was with Mr. Simatovic and another colonel when we greeted each other and spent a couple of minutes next to each other, somewhere near Kladusa in that Cazin Krajina. I've already spoken about that and I've told you that I saw those Red Berets on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I'm looking at the clock. I don't know whether this would be a suitable time to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can I just ask one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Colonel Sajic, who was he? Lieutenant-colonel Sajic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of him but I can't put the name to a face.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And also not to a position, may I take it? Sometimes you know what position someone holds without knowing his face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what his position was. I don't know what he looked like. I only heard his name as part of that story about the creation of a common state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak to anyone about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or even testimony you've given earlier in this case, and testimony still to be given because we'd like to see you back tomorrow at 9.00. Could the witness first be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I'd just like to inquire where we are in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think two hours should do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would just remain within the time-limits. So you are expected tomorrow to finish in two hours because you've used three hours now, you would scheduled five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So shortly after the first break tomorrow morning, because we adjourn until tomorrow, Wednesday, the 7th of December, 9.00 in the morning in this same Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 7th day of December, 2011 at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.02 p.m.
